This post is intended as an end to end demonstration of the Resgo probabilistic prospect evaluation toolkit, and my motivations for building it.

Resgo is my attempt to make prospect evaluation probabilistic all the way down—uncertain geology, uncertain field development performance, uncertain economics—all in an integrated simulation model.

It is desigend for probabilistic assessment of exploration and early development opportunities, preserving uncertainty from subsurface volumes through to commercial outcomes.

It does this by integrating volumetrics, field production, and commercial modelling in a single vectorized model, optimized for highly iterative, scenario based workloads.

Motivations

Resgo encapsulates my approach to technical work and the general idea of “informatics”. Reporting a single number NPV for a project as complex as an oil and gas field development, ahead of drilling, is not a good idea. There is no single number that captures the uncertainty (and exposure) inherent in such a complex undertaking, so the decision appropriate information is not a point estimate, but a series of distributions that capture the uncertainties involved.

Traditionally these uncertainties are almost impossible to integrate end to end. Static volumetric models feeding into dynamic simulation models very rarely propagate uncertainty up the chain through to economic modelling. The undertaking is simply too slow and clumsy to be done.

Resgo provides that integration. It does so by making some simplifying assumptions about reservoir behaviour, but in low information contexts—before drilling or early in field development—I would argue that simpler models are more appropriate. Not because they model reservoir physics rigorously (that would require dynamic simulation), but because they are flexible enough to configure quickly, and iterate on.

This will become clear with an example.

Example

The following example is for a large, stacked reservoir field development, with 9 target reservoirs and 25 planned producers.

Volumetric Simulation

Resgo models begin with a stochastic volumetric simulation of each reservoir, separated into Oil, Gas, Solution Gas and Condensate in place. The Solution Gas and Condensate are derived from the Oil and Gas volumes and their respective Fluid GOR/CGR distributions. Reservoirs can be single phase or separated into oil and gas legs via a Gas Cap Fraction parameter.

Each reservoir and fluid parameter is represented with a probability distribution, with flexible copula models used to capture correlations between them. A few examples are shown below:

Each reservoir in the simulated stack has a series of risk factors applied, which together with a dependency parameter (capturing the correlation of risk across reservoirs) is used to simulate the success or failure of each targeted reservoir.

Here are the individual zone success case oil volumes:

And the overall total visualized with an ECDF plot:

The Total STOIIP in the example shown above represents the simulated range of STOIIP outcomes across simulated trials. The geological risk factor of each individual Zone is visualized here as the y-intercept of each ECDF.

Field Development Simulation

Resgo is designed to support multi-well developments, as realistic end to end economic modelling is not achievable without a simulation of multiple wells producing a field, with the CAPEX/OPEX associated with each.

This includes complex phased developments targetting multiple reservoirs with oil and gas caps at different stages of development. Producers can be scheduled specifically, with defined drill and online dates, or they can be automatically sequenced on a defined cadence, coming online after an assumed drill-to-online period.

The field production simulation utilizes Decline Curve Analysis (DCA) formulae in a stochastic model, constrained by static volumes (simulated in the volumetric model), initial rate and recovery factor distributions. The model is configured to ensure that the produced volumes in a given month are consistent with each producer’s share of the reservoir volumes it produces from in that month. This means that the total field production (Ultimate Recovery) across all producers will be consistent with the Ultimate Recovery implied by the static volume multiplied by the recovery factor for that reservoir.

This consistency guarantee is what makes Resgo so powerful. It is a physically consistent, stochastic material balance simulation of the field that runs in seconds.

Dynamic simulation modelling traditionally takes weeks of configuration, and hours to run. This makes iteration extremely inefficient. Resgo can simulate hundreds of different scenarios, each taking seconds, to fully explore the optionality of field development.

The oil and gas streams are plotted as stochastic time series plots, showing wells coming online through the development of the field.

As more wells are brought online, the decline of the field steepens as more producers exploit the shared resource. The simulation also “cancels” planned wells dynamically when remaining field volumes do not justify continued development. This avoids unfairly penalizing results with unrealistic poor decision making, which feeds into economics.

All field production results are fed directly into the economic model, so options are assessed on their commercial basis, not proxies of it like EUR or STOIIP.

Economic Simulation

In this phase we set price, royalty, tax, opex/capex assumptions, then run economics on top of production.

The Resgo economic model runs full OPEX/CAPEX, royalty, tax, financing, price and depreciation modelling, fully integrated with the rest of the stochastic model upstream.

It includes configurable tax and royalty schemes, as well as optional correlated oil and gas price stochastic forecasting using Geometric Brownian Motion or Ornstein Uhlenbeck mean reverting stochastic processes.

This flexibility allows full stochastic analysis through to commercial metrics like IRR, NPV, PI, and payback time.

Below, nominal discounted cash flows are shown, which sum to project NPV.

The cumulative discounted flows shown in the bottom chart here reflect the project value through time, with NPV being the end of project distribution of cumulative cash flows.

Decision Analysis

  • Provide decision metrics for whether the opportunity should be pursued or not.

Why do I report such wide confidence intervals?

As a habit I visualize wide uncertainty ranges, from P99 to P1. The reason I do this is simple: hundreds of millions of dollars are on the line. I don’t want to be 90% sure that a project requiring me to commit a billion dollars of capital will make a return, I want to be 99.99% sure. If I don’t have that luxury, fine, but showing that I do in fact have it, is extremely valuable, as it means a safe decision can be made. These models should enable more effective decision making, a P90-P10 range is not a sufficient description. I want to know what happens if shit completely hits the fan! If there is a real possibility of losing money, I want to know how much, and how likely we think that is. Point metrics provide none of this.

The other reason is that often people consider probabilistic analyses as worthless because all the uncertainties stack up to something approximating “we have no bloody idea what will happen”. This is a possible result of a stochastic analysis (and if it’s a good one, you should probably take it seriously and avoid doing anything drastic), but much more often the uncertainties flow through into something that actually represents a good representative range of outcomes.

Uncertainties don’t blow up into infinite doubt as you stack them—they converge. Correlation across uncertain quantities complicates this somewhat, but the correlations are rarely so dramatic that uncertainty blows up. Being explicit about the range the model produces (through wide confidence intervals, probability visualisations or whatever else) is a mark of confidence that the range it is producing is actually meaningful.

And if your uncertainty range is well defined, and never crosses “we go bankrupt”, or (less dramatically) “we lose money”, that is very valuable information.

Because decision making under uncertainty is not “project A has a higher NPV than project B, so let’s do A”, it is “project A exposes us to financial ruin, project B is a safe bet. So let’s do B”.

Ignoring uncertainty in decision making is insane. Glossing over uncertainty with poorly constrained metrics is not good enough.

Back of the envelope, or throwing the whole textbook

Resgo can be a “back of the envelope” exercise on steroids, as it allows a technical team to see the consequences of their assumptions propagate all the way through to commercial outcomes in seconds. A geologist might argue that a reservoir is much riskier than previously supposed, and 10 seconds later can have their opinion reflected in project NPV. This creates laser focus in a technical team, as what really matters is identifiable in seconds, instead of argued about for months.

The model can be calibrated rigorously based on geostatistical offset analysis, or it can be run on lower effort back of the envelope assumptions. Either way, the information put into the model will flow through to its logical consequences. Add high confidence assumptions, get tighter commercial results.

That configurability means that new information is also very easy to integrate into the analysis. New reservoir data, new offset analyses, new analogues, new commercial information—just rerun the model. It will only take 10 seconds.

Just add information until a decision can be made. Then make the decision.

Future Plans

Resgo is currenly a backend tool that I use in a consultancy capacity. It is not yet a standalone offering. It may become one eventually, but I am focussed on working on data platform offerings ahead of specialized analytical tools for now.

That being said, it integrates very well with a good data system, and my intention for deployments would be to utilize the GIS database and geostatistical modelling to infer appropriate distributions for properties using well offsets where available.

Prospect evaluation occurs in many different information contexts, often very information poor ones. Flexibility is key, so it sits comfortably on its own, rolled out when I need it.
